newsitem.title: CONGO: Looting in central Brazzaville, bodies in streets.
newsitem.headline: Looting in central Brazzaville, bodies in streets.

text.p: Gunfire rattled through Brazzaville for a sixth day on Tuesday as French soldiers moved through the Congolese capital rescuing foreigners trapped by fighting between government troops and a political militia.
The United States Defence Department said it had sent a small team to Brazzaville to assess the situation in case an evacuation of Americans is requested.
Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said the team of about a dozen specialists, security troops and planners was already in Brazzaville but no decision had been made on evacuations.

Bloody street battles between soldiers and militiamen loyal to Republic of Congo President Pascal Lissouba and a militia loyal to ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso have flared and subsided through the city centre since Thursday.
On Tuesday fighting raged close to the international airport, preventing a charter that was to ferry people to Kinshasa, capital of neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo, from taking off.
Residents said scores of bloated bodies lay uncollected in the streets. Looting had spread from other districts to the capital's central commercial area, they added.
One report said among businesses looted was the city's largest supermarket, Score, close to the American embassy.
"I saw dozens and dozens of bodies rotting on (the main) Avenue de la Paix," a resident said after fleeing to Kinshasa.
"Most of them appeared to be civilians, mostly women and children who were caught in the crossfire," he said.
He reported a similar scene from the western suburb of Batignolles. "There were also many bodies (there) and houses abandoned after looting."
Sporadic mortar fire echoed across the city more than two hours after Brazzaville Mayor Bernard Kolelas met Lissouba and the mayor's spokesman said a three-hour truce had been agreed.
Hundreds of Congolese civilians took refuge in the Bacongo suburb, fief of a neutral militia loyal to Kolelas, who has offered to mediate between the two sides.
Truckloads of people who were unable to find shelter in Bacongo headed for interior villages.
Congo's foreign minister meanwhile ruled out any negotiation with Sassou Nguesso and state radio broadcast a statement by the military high command calling on the people to support the army.
"Nothing is negotiable," Destin Arsene Tsaty-Mboungou told a news conference.

Tsaty-Mboungou said the only way out of the crisis was outside mediation to create conditions for a planned July 27 presidential election in which Lisouba and Sassou Nguesso could square off peacefully.
Asked what had become of an accord which French President Jacques Chirac's office said had been reached with both sides for a ceasefire, Tsaty-Mboungou replied:
"No. For the time being the fire has not ceased. It continues to kill in Brazzaville but I hope that the appeals for peace which were made will be heard by both sides."
Political and ethnic conflict killed 2,000 people in the capital in 1993 and has exploded again as Congo approaches a presidential election set for July 27.

The government, enforcing a crackdown on private militias after clashes in the north, sent troops on Thursday to surround the home of Sassou Nguesso, who lost the last presidential election to Lissouba in 1992.
In Brazzaville on Tuesday, light armoured cars protected convoys of civilian vehicles driven by French, Lebanese and other expatriate volunteers as they moved to different parts of the city centre.
France has sent 400 troops to reinforce the 450 already in Brazzaville, where they were dispatched in March in case foreigners needed to be evacuated from Kinshasa.
French embassy officials said between 700 and 800 foreigners were flown out of Brazzaville on Monday in military transport planes to the Gabon capital Libreville.
They said more than 1,000 French citizens could still be in the Brazzaville area.
